core_summary: This chapter introduces geometric construction using ruler, compass, and set-squares. Students transition from freehand sketches to technical constructions, exploring circles, radii, diameters, center points, length transfers, perpendiculars, rectangles, and squares. The chapter establishes circle boundary equidistance (every boundary point lies at distance r from center O), d = 2r, concentric circles, and compass length transfer to eliminate ruler tick parallax errors. Set-squares (45°-45°-90° and 30°-60°-90°) construct precise 90° right angles, and compass radius step-transfers construct regular inscribed hexagons.
key_concepts: Geometric Precision and Technical Tools: Moving from freehand drawing to technical construction requires specialized tools: Ruler (measuring linear distances), Compass (drawing circles and locking distance spans), Set-squares (constructing exact 90° right angles).
Circle Definition and Equidistance Property: A circle is the set of all points in a plane equidistant from a fixed center point O. The constant boundary distance is the Radius r.
Radius and Diameter Relationship: A line segment passing through the center connecting two boundary points is a Diameter d. Relationship: d = 2r, or r = d / 2.

Concentric Circles Construction: Concentric circles share the exact same central point O but have different radius lengths (r1 != r2). Constructed by keeping the compass needle fixed at O while adjusting radius openings.

Transferring Segment Lengths with Compass: Transferring line segment lengths using a compass span is more accurate than ruler measurement because it eliminates visual parallax tick mark reading errors.

Constructing Perpendicular Lines with Set-Squares: A set-square contains an exact 90° corner. Aligning one set-square leg along a baseline and drawing along the adjacent perpendicular leg constructs precise right angles.

Constructing Rectangles and Squares: A rectangle is constructed by drawing a baseline segment, erecting perpendicular rays at both endpoints using set-squares, marking width lengths along perpendiculars, and joining top endpoints.

Inscribing Regular Hexagons via Radius Steps: Maintaining a compass opening at radius r and stepping consecutive arcs around a circle boundary divides the circle into 6 equal segments, constructing a regular inscribed hexagon.
Arc Intersections and Unique Point Location: Two intersecting circular arcs define precise single geometric points in a plane.
Symmetry in Geometric Constructions: Maintaining constant compass openings guarantees congruent side lengths and symmetrical geometric structures.
Perpendicular Bisector Intuition: The locus of points equidistant from two endpoints A and B forms the perpendicular bisector of segment AB.

Engineering and Architectural Drafting Applications: Technical geometric construction principles underpin architectural blueprints, mechanical engineering drafts, and computer-aided design (CAD) systems.

key_terms.definition: A closed plane curve consisting of all points equidistant from a fixed center point.
The fixed internal reference point from which all points on a circle boundary are equidistant.
The fixed distance from the center point of a circle to any point on its boundary.
A straight line segment passing through the center of a circle with both endpoints on the circumference (d = 2r).
Circles of different radii that share the exact same central reference point.
A geometric instrument with a needle leg and pencil leg used for drawing circles and transferring lengths.
A triangular drawing tool featuring an exact 90° right angle used for constructing perpendicular lines.
Two lines or segments intersecting at an exact 90-degree right angle.
A continuous portion of the circumference of a circle.
A polygon whose vertices all lie on the boundary circumference of a circle.
The process of locking a segment length using a compass span to replicate it elsewhere without numerical reading errors.
The enclosed outer boundary curve length of a circle.

key_takeaways: A circle consists of all points equidistant from a central reference point O.
Diameter d equals twice the radius r (d = 2r).
Concentric circles share the same center point but possess different radius lengths.
Transferring segment lengths using a compass span eliminates ruler tick parallax errors.
Set-squares feature an exact 90° right angle corner for constructing perpendicular lines.
Rectangles and squares are constructed by erecting perpendiculars at baseline endpoints.
Stepping compass radius r around a circle boundary constructs an inscribed regular hexagon.
Intersecting arcs locate exact geometric points on a drafting plane.
Compass needle pressure must remain at the central pivot handle to avoid radius slippage.
Geometric construction principles form the foundation of engineering blueprints and CAD.
